pos: n. (a Hebrew liquid measure, about the tenth of an homer)
etymology: Hebrew bath, a liquid measure, the exact counterpart of the dry ephah. Nothing whatever to do with washing: the KJV bath is a vessel of capacity, and Ezekiel makes God himself legislate its size.
biblical_def: The bath is the standard liquid measure of Israel, and Scripture uses it where quantities are being counted honestly. Solomon's molten sea “contained two thousand baths” (1 Kings 7:26). In the timber contract with Hiram the king promises “twenty thousand measures of beaten wheat, and twenty thousand measures of barley, and twenty thousand baths of wine” (2 Chronicles 2:10), and Artaxerxes' decree for the temple allows “an hundred baths of wine, and to an hundred baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much” (Ezra 7:22). The theological weight falls on Ezekiel, where the restored order begins with a law about measuring cups: “The ephah and the bath shall be of one measure, that the bath may contain the tenth part of an homer, and the ephah the tenth part of an homer: the measure thereof shall be after the homer” (Ezekiel 45:11). Dry and liquid are bound to one standard so that no man can profit by the difference. A God who regulates the size of a wine measure in a vision of the age to come is a God who takes commerce seriously.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives bath as a Hebrew measure containing the tenth of an homer, or about seven gallons and four pints of liquids, as wine or oil.
webster_full: BATH, n. A Hebrew measure containing the tenth of an homer, or seven gallons and four pints, as a measure for liquids.
HOMER, n. A Hebrew measure of about eight bushels or seventy-five gallons; the largest of the Hebrew measures.
EPHAH, n. A Hebrew measure of three pecks and three pints, or, according to others, of seven gallons and four pints.
MEASURE, n. That by which extent or dimension is ascertained; a standard of quantity; a rule by which any thing is adjusted.
JUST, a. Regular; orderly; exactly proportioned; as, a just weight and a just measure.
scriptures: 1 Kings 7:26
And it was an hand breadth thick, and the brim thereof was wrought like the brim of a cup, with flowers of lilies: it contained two thousand baths.
2 Chronicles 2:10

And, behold, I will give to thy servants, the hewers that cut timber, twenty thousand measures of beaten wheat, and twenty thousand measures of barley, and twenty thousand baths of wine, and twenty thousand baths of oil.
Ezra 7:22
Unto an hundred talents of silver, and to an hundred measures of wheat, and to an hundred baths of wine, and to an hundred baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much. measures: Chaldee, cors
Ezekiel 45:11
The ephah and the bath shall be of one measure, that the bath may contain the tenth part of an homer, and the ephah the tenth part of an homer: the measure thereof shall be after the homer.
corruption_summary: Weights and measures are treated as a technical matter beneath religion, when Scripture makes a standard measure a point of holiness and puts the regulation of the bath into a prophet's vision of the restored temple.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern piety divides life into a spiritual part and a commercial part and expects God to be interested in the first. Ezekiel 45 refuses the division. In the middle of a vision of the temple, the altar and the prince, the prophet is given the dimensions of a measuring vessel and told that the dry measure and the liquid measure shall be of one standard. The law against divers weights and divers measures is not a footnote to holiness; a man who shortens a bath of oil has broken with God as really as a man who neglects a sacrifice, and Scripture says so in the same breath.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honesty of a fixed standard. A bath is the tenth of an homer because God said so, not because a trade guild agreed on it, and the size of the cup is therefore not negotiable by the man holding it. Every generation invents ways to keep two measures — one for what it buys and another for what it sells, one for judging itself and another for judging its neighbour. The remedy is an external standard a man did not set and cannot adjust.
roots_summary: Hebrew bath (H1324), a liquid measure; chomer (H2563), a homer; ephah (H374), the dry counterpart; middah (H4060), measure or extent.
roots_lines: Hebrew bath (H1324) — the bath, a liquid measure, the tenth of an homer.
Hebrew chomer (H2563) — a homer, the largest Hebrew measure; the standard both ephah and bath answer to.
Hebrew ephah (H374) — the dry measure bound by Ezekiel to the same homer as the bath.
Hebrew middah (H4060) — measure, extent, portion; the general word for a fixed standard.
Hebrew eben (H68) — a stone, hence a weight; divers weights are an abomination to the LORD.
usage: “It contained two thousand baths” — the molten sea measured honestly.
“An hundred baths of wine” — a pagan king's decree for God's house.
“The ephah and the bath shall be of one measure” — one standard for dry and wet.

pos: n. & a. (a row or line; order of battle; also, luxuriant, full-grown)
etymology: Old French ranc, a row or line. The Authorized Version carries two distinct senses under the one spelling: the military rank, a line of men holding formation, and the older adjective meaning rank in growth — the fat, full ears of Pharaoh's dream.
biblical_def: The adjective comes first, in a dream that would feed a nation: “And he slept and dreamed the second time: and, behold, seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk, rank and good” (Genesis 41:5) — the Hebrew is literally fat, and the seven lean ears that devour them are the famine. The noun is military and appears where Israel marches in order: the camp of Ephraim “shall go forward in the third rank” (Numbers 2:24). It also describes building — in Solomon's house “there were windows in three rows, and light was against light in three ranks” (1 Kings 7:4). The finest use is a commendation of Zebulun at David's coronation: “such as went forth to battle, expert in war, with all instruments of war, fifty thousand, which could keep rank: they were not of double heart” (1 Chronicles 12:33). The chronicler joins the two things as if they were one thing, because they are: men who keep rank in the line are men who are not double in the heart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rank as a row or line, particularly of soldiers standing abreast; and as an adjective, luxuriant in growth, strong-scented, exuberant.
webster_full: RANK, n. A row or line, applied to troops; a line of men standing abreast or side by side, and as opposed to file.
RANK, n. Degree of dignity, eminence or excellence; as, a writer of the first rank.
RANK, a. Luxuriant in growth; being of vigorous growth; as, rank grass; rank corn.
RANK, a. Strong to the taste or smell; rancid; strong-scented.
ORDER, n. Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; a state in which things bear a due relation to each other.
scriptures: Genesis 41:5
And he slept and dreamed the second time: and, behold, seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk, rank and good.
Numbers 2:24
All that were numbered of the camp of Ephraim were an hundred thousand and eight thousand and an hundred, throughout their armies. And they shall go forward in the third rank.
1 Kings 7:4
And there were windows in three rows, and light was against light in three ranks. light
1 Chronicles 12:33
Of Zebulun, such as went forth to battle, expert in war, with all instruments of war, fifty thousand, which could keep rank: they were not of double heart.
corruption_summary: Rank in the sense of ordered place is treated as inherently oppressive, so that any arrangement of men in ranks is suspected of injustice; Scripture makes keeping rank a virtue and ties it directly to an undivided heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning assumption is that hierarchy as such is the problem and that flattening every order is progress. Scripture does not share it. Israel marched by ranks because a mass is not an army, and the chronicler names keeping rank among the qualifications of Zebulun's fifty thousand alongside their expertness in war. God's own house was built with its windows in three ranks. Order is not the enemy of love; disorder is, because a body whose members will not keep their place cannot move together or protect its weakest.

What Scripture does condemn is rank abused — place used to devour rather than to guard. The corrective is in the same verse as the commendation: they were not of double heart. A man who keeps rank with a divided heart is worse than a man out of rank, because he has borrowed the credit of order to serve himself. The principle to recover is that rank is a station of service under authority, held by men whose hearts are single, and that Pharaoh's rank and good ears were a gift of God before they were a store of grain.
roots_summary: Hebrew bariy (H1277), fat, plump; degel (H1714), a standard or banner; maarakah (H4634), a battle array; tur (H2905), a row.
roots_lines: Hebrew bariy (H1277) — fat, well-fed; the rank and good ears of Pharaoh's dream.
Hebrew degel (H1714) — a standard, the banner each camp marched under in its rank.
Hebrew maarakah (H4634) — a row, an array, the order of battle.
Hebrew tur (H2905) — a row or course; the three ranks of windows in Solomon's house.
Hebrew lo leb valeb — literally not of a heart and a heart; the undivided men who could keep rank.
usage: “Seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk, rank and good” — the older sense.
“They shall go forward in the third rank” — an army, not a crowd.
“Which could keep rank: they were not of double heart” — the two go together.

pos: n. (something joined or annexed; an ornamental appendage)
etymology: Latin additio, from addere, to put to. The word occurs only three times in the Authorized Version, all three in one chapter, and all three describing the ornamental work cast into the ten brasen bases of Solomon's temple.
biblical_def: The whole biblical career of this word is spent in a foundry. Describing the bases that carried the lavers, the chronicler of Kings writes: “And on the borders that were between the ledges were lions, oxen, and cherubims: and upon the ledges there was a base above: and beneath the lions and oxen were certain additions made of thin work” (1 Kings 7:29). The additions are placed again in the next verse — “under the laver were undersetters molten, at the side of every addition” (1 Kings 7:30) — and once more among the graven cherubims, lions and palm trees, “according to the proportion of every one, and additions round about” (1 Kings 7:36). They are appendages of thin work, added beauty on a thing already finished, in a place where almost nobody would see them. That Scripture records them at all is the point. The same God who forbids adding to his word (Deuteronomy 4:2) filled his house with additions of beaten brass, because the two kinds of adding are opposite acts.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines addition as the act of adding; anything added; and in law, a title annexed to a man's name to show his rank or occupation.
webster_full: ADDITION, n. The act of adding, opposed to subtraction or diminution; as, a sum is increased by addition.
ADDITION, n. Any thing added, whether material or immaterial; an appendage.
ADDITION, n. In music, a dot at the side of a note, to lengthen its sound one half.
ORNAMENT, n. That which embellishes; something which, added to another thing, renders it more beautiful to the eye.
APPENDAGE, n. Something added to a principal or greater thing, though not necessary to it.
scriptures: 1 Kings 7:29
And on the borders that were between the ledges were lions, oxen, and cherubims: and upon the ledges there was a base above: and beneath the lions and oxen were certain additions made of thin work.
1 Kings 7:30
And every base had four brasen wheels, and plates of brass: and the four corners thereof had undersetters: under the laver were undersetters molten, at the side of every addition.
1 Kings 7:36
For on the plates of the ledges thereof, and on the borders thereof, he graved cherubims, lions, and palm trees, according to the proportion of every one, and additions round about.
Deuteronomy 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
corruption_summary: Adding to God's revelation is defended as development and sensitivity to the age, while adding beauty to God's house is dismissed as waste — an exact inversion of the two kinds of addition Scripture distinguishes.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture draws a hard line at one kind of addition: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deuteronomy 4:2). Every generation finds a respectable name for crossing it — development, contextualization, new light, the leading of the Spirit beyond the text — and the effect is always the same, that something not given by God acquires the authority of God. The confessional principle stands: what is added to the rule of faith is not an enrichment of it but a rival to it.

The inverted error is a churchliness that treats every beauty as waste. 1 Kings 7 records additions of thin work cast beneath lions and oxen on the base of a laver, and preserves the detail for three thousand years. The God who would not have a syllable added to his word had cherubim and palm trees and additions round about wrought into the furniture of his house. Craft and cost spent on the worship of God are not extravagance, and the woman with the alabaster box heard her waste called a good work.
roots_summary: Hebrew loyah (H3914), a wreath or appendage; miktsoa (H4740), an angle or corner-piece; yasaph (H3254), to add; garah (H1639), to diminish.
roots_lines: Hebrew loyah (H3914) — a wreath, a garland-like appendage; the additions of thin work in 1 Kings 7:29.
Hebrew maaseh morad — work of descent, thin or hanging work; how the additions were cast.
Hebrew yasaph (H3254) — to add, to increase; the forbidden verb of Deuteronomy 4:2.
Hebrew garah (H1639) — to diminish, to take away; the twin prohibition beside adding.
Hebrew mekonah (H4350) — a base, a stand; the ten brasen bases that carried the lavers.
usage: “Certain additions made of thin work” — beauty where few would look.
“At the side of every addition” — recorded three thousand years.
“Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you” — the other kind of adding.

pos: n. (one who writes; a scribe or recorder)
etymology: Old English writere, from writan, to score or incise. The Authorized Version uses it five times, and the writer in view is never a literary man but an officer: a muster-officer with a pen, a recorder of chronicles, and the man in linen with the inkhorn at his side in Ezekiel's vision.
biblical_def: Deborah's song counts the writers among the fighting tribes: “out of Zebulun they that handle the pen of the writer” (Judges 5:14) — the pen stands in a list of weapons and commanders, because a people that can record and muster can also war. David's court had its recorder, rendered in the margin “writer of chronicles” (2 Samuel 8:16). The psalmist, overflowing with a song about the King, reaches for the same figure: “my tongue is the pen of a ready writer” (Psalm 45:1). And in the most solemn use, judgment on Jerusalem begins with a man carrying stationery: among six men with slaughter weapons was “one man among them... clothed with linen, with a writer's inkhorn by his side” (Ezekiel 9:2), and it is this writer, not the swordsmen, who goes first, to set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and cry for the abominations done in the city. The pen precedes the sword, and it decides who is spared.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a writer as one who writes or has written; a scribe; a clerk; and an author.
webster_full: WRITER, n. One who writes or has written. A scribe; a clerk; one who is employed in writing.
WRITER, n. An author; one who composes or writes a book or treatise.
SCRIBE, n. In Scripture and the Jewish history, a clerk or secretary to the king; also, a writer and a doctor of the law.
PEN, n. An instrument used for writing, usually made of a quill, but sometimes of other material.
INKHORN, n. A small vessel used to hold ink, formerly made of horn, and carried at the girdle.
scriptures: Judges 5:14
Out of Ephraim was there a root of them against Amalek; after thee, Benjamin, among thy people; out of Machir came down governors, and out of Zebulun they that handle the pen of the writer.
Psalm 45:1

To the chief Musician upon Shoshannim, for the sons of Korah, Maschil, A Song of loves. My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer.
Ezekiel 9:2

And, behold, six men came from the way of the higher gate, which lieth toward the north, and every man a slaughter weapon in his hand; and one man among them was clothed with linen, with a writer's inkhorn by his side: and they went in, and stood beside the brasen altar.
Ezekiel 9:3

And the glory of the God of Israel was gone up from the cherub, whereupon he was, to the threshold of the house. And he called to the man clothed with linen, which had the writer's inkhorn by his side;
corruption_summary: Writing is prized now for self-expression and reach, while Scripture presents the writer as an officer under authority whose record serves a King and, in Ezekiel, decides who is marked and spared.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern writer is understood by his voice: what he has to say, how distinctively he says it, how many hear it. Every biblical writer is understood by his commission. Zebulun's pen-handlers are named among the tribes that came to the battle; the recorder writes the chronicles of a king, not of himself; the man with the inkhorn writes only what he is sent to write. Psalm 45:1 is the exception that proves it — the psalmist's heart is indeed overflowing, but the matter is touching the king, and the ready pen is at the service of a subject greater than the writer.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the seriousness of the record. In Ezekiel 9 the writer goes through the city before the executioners, and his mark is the difference between life and death. Words written down outlast the man who wrote them and shape what those who come after believe. That is a reason for care, for accuracy, and for writing under authority rather than merely out of oneself — and it is why the church has always cared what her writers put in ink.
roots_summary: Hebrew caphar (H5608), to count, to recount, hence to write; copher (H5608), a scribe; et (H5842), a stylus or pen; qeceth (H7083), an inkhorn.
roots_lines: Hebrew caphar (H5608) — to score, to count, to recount; the root behind scribe and writer alike.
Hebrew copher (H5608) — a scribe, an enumerator, a muster-officer; the writer of Judges 5:14.
Hebrew et (H5842) — a stylus or pen; the pen of a ready writer in Psalm 45:1.
Hebrew qeceth (H7083) — an inkhorn; carried by the man clothed with linen in Ezekiel 9.
Hebrew mahiyr (H4106) — skilful, prompt, ready; the readiness of the psalmist's pen.
usage: “They that handle the pen of the writer” — counted among the men of war.
“My tongue is the pen of a ready writer” — a pen at the King's service.
“With a writer's inkhorn by his side” — the pen goes before the sword.

pos: n. (the reed of the Nile; a substance to write upon)
etymology: Greek papuros, the papyrus reed of the Nile, through Latin papyrus. The Authorized Version uses the word twice, once for the living reed in an Egyptian marsh and once for the sheet an apostle declines to use.
biblical_def: Isaiah's oracle against Egypt strikes at the Nile itself, and with it the industry that grew on its banks: “The paper reeds by the brooks, by the mouth of the brooks, and every thing sown by the brooks, shall wither, be driven away, and be no more” (Isaiah 19:7). Egypt's paper, like Egypt's grain, depended on a river God could dry. The second use is one of the warmest verses in the New Testament, and it sets paper in its proper rank: “Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full” (2 John 1:12). John, who wrote a gospel, three epistles and the Revelation, tells a congregation that there are things he will not commit to paper because presence is better. Writing is a gift and a necessity, and the apostle who used it most says plainly that it is second best to a face.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines paper as a substance formed into thin sheets for writing, from the ancient Egyptian papyrus, a plant of the reed kind growing on the Nile.
webster_full: PAPER, n. A substance formed into thin sheets, on which letters and figures are written or printed.
PAPER, n. The ancient paper was made of the papyrus, a reed growing on the banks of the Nile in Egypt.
PAPYRUS, n. A plant of the reed kind, growing in Egypt, of which the ancients made paper.
INK, n. A black liquor or substance used for writing, generally made of an infusion of galls with copperas and gum arabic.
EPISTLE, n. A writing, directed or sent, communicating intelligence to a distant person; a letter.
scriptures: Isaiah 19:7
The paper reeds by the brooks, by the mouth of the brooks, and every thing sown by the brooks, shall wither, be driven away, and be no more.
2 John 1:12
Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full.
3 John 1:13
I had many things to write, but I will not with ink and pen write unto thee:
2 Corinthians 3:3

Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart.
corruption_summary: An age of endless text has made the written word the default and the face the exception, reversing an apostle's plain judgment that paper and ink are the substitute and presence is the thing.
corruption_paragraphs: It is now normal for whole relationships, whole churches and whole controversies to be conducted on a screen, and the written word has quietly become the primary mode of dealing with people rather than the emergency one. 2 John 1:12 states the apostolic order the other way round: John had many things to write, and would not write them, because he trusted to come and speak face to face — and the reason he gives is joy, that our joy may be full. Correspondence carries information; presence carries fulness. A congregation fed only from a distance is being kept alive on what the apostle called second best.

Paul supplies the deeper point in 2 Corinthians 3:3, where the letter that matters is not written with ink at all but with the Spirit of the living God, not in tables of stone but in fleshy tables of the heart. Paper perishes — Isaiah watched Egypt's reeds wither by the brooks and be no more. What God writes he writes in men. The principle to recover is that the aim of every letter, sermon and page is a living epistle, and that no quantity of text substitutes for a pastor who comes.
roots_summary: Hebrew arowth (H6169), bare places or paper reeds; yeor (H2975), the Nile; Greek chartes (G5489), a sheet of paper; melan (G3188), ink.
roots_lines: Hebrew arowth (H6169) — paper reeds, meadows by a river; what withered in Isaiah 19:7.
Hebrew yeor (H2975) — the Nile, the river Egypt's paper and grain both depended on.
Greek chartes (G5489) — a sheet of papyrus paper; the paper John would not use.
Greek melan (G3188) — ink, literally the black; paired with paper in 2 John.
Greek epistole (G1992) — a letter; and in 2 Corinthians 3, the saints themselves as Christ's epistle.
usage: “The paper reeds by the brooks... shall wither” — Egypt's industry dried up.
“I would not write with paper and ink” — an apostle preferring a face.
“That our joy may be full” — the reason presence outranks correspondence.

etymology: Old English sprecan, to speak. The noun occurs twice in the Authorized Version, and the two uses are a study in contrast: an evil speaker the psalmist asks God to unseat, and the chief speaker whom a pagan city mistook for a god.
biblical_def: David prays against a man defined by his mouth: “Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth: evil shall hunt the violent man to overthrow him” (Psalm 140:11). The petition is that such a man should not be established — not merely that he be silenced, but that he never acquire a settled place from which to speak. The New Testament use is at Lystra, where a healing brought the crowd out with garlands: “And they called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker” (Acts 14:12). Facility with words drew the divine honour, and Paul's response was to rend his clothes and run in among them crying that they were men of like passions. The two verses set the biblical estimate of the gifted tongue: it is a real power, capable of establishing a man or of getting him worshipped, and it is therefore the faculty most in need of a governor.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a speaker as one who speaks; one who utters or pronounces a discourse; and the presiding officer of a deliberative assembly.
webster_full: SPEAKER, n. One that speaks, in whatever manner. One who utters or pronounces a discourse; usually, one who utters a speech in public.
SPEAKER, n. The presiding officer of a legislative body, so called because he speaks or promulgates the will of the house.
SPOKESMAN, n. One who speaks for another; one who is deputed to speak in the name of another.
ELOQUENCE, n. The act or art of speaking well; oratory; the power of expressing strong emotions in striking language.
SLANDER, n. A false tale or report maliciously uttered, tending to injure the reputation of another.
scriptures: Psalm 140:11
Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth: evil shall hunt the violent man to overthrow him.
Acts 14:12
And they called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker.
Acts 14:15

And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:
James 3:5
Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!
corruption_summary: The culture measures a speaker by reach and effect, so that a man who can hold a crowd is credited with authority; Scripture treats the same facility as a power to be feared, and asks that the evil speaker never be established.
corruption_paragraphs: Platforms are now awarded for the ability to command attention, and the church has borrowed the standard. A man who speaks well is assumed to have something worth saying, and a hearing is granted on the strength of the delivery. Lystra made exactly that mistake in its purest form: Paul was the chief speaker, therefore Paul was Mercurius, and the oxen and garlands were already at the gates. Paul's reaction is the model — he rent his clothes, he denied the honour, he insisted he was a man of like passions, and he turned the crowd from vanities to the living God.

Psalm 140:11 asks something sharper still: that the evil speaker not be established in the earth. It is a prayer against permanence — against the slanderer acquiring an institution, a following, a settled seat. James says the tongue is a little member that boasteth great things, and Scripture never treats speech as merely expressive. It builds and it burns. The recovery is to weigh speakers by the truth of what they say and the holiness of how they live, and to pray that God would refuse a lasting foothold to the men whose gift is only their mouth.
roots_summary: Hebrew ish lashon, a man of tongue; kun (H3559), to establish; Greek logos (G3056), word or speech; hegeomai (G2233), to lead, hence chief.
roots_lines: Hebrew ish lashon — literally a man of tongue; the evil speaker of Psalm 140:11.
Hebrew kun (H3559) — to set up, establish, make firm; what David asks God to withhold.
Greek logos (G3056) — word, speech, discourse; the substance a speaker is judged by.
Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to lead the way; behind the phrase the chief speaker at Lystra.
Greek glossa (G1100) — the tongue; a little member that boasteth great things.
usage: “Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth” — a prayer against permanence.
“Because he was the chief speaker” — and they brought oxen and garlands.
“We also are men of like passions with you” — the apostolic refusal.

pos: n. (a cause pleaded; a suit at law)
etymology: Old French plai, from Latin placitum, that which is decreed. The word occurs once in the Authorized Version, in the law that establishes a supreme court for Israel, where it names one of the three classes of hard cases.
biblical_def: Moses provides for cases the local gate cannot settle: “If there arise a matter too hard for thee in judgment, between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke, being matters of controversy within thy gates: then shalt thou arise, and get thee up into the place which the LORD thy God shall choose” (Deuteronomy 17:8). Three categories are named — blood and blood (capital cases), plea and plea (civil suits), stroke and stroke (cases of assault or of leprous plague) — and the provision for each is the same: a higher court sitting at the sanctuary, whose sentence Israel was to obey without declining to the right hand or to the left. The word therefore carries the whole idea of a cause honestly brought and honestly heard. Job uses the same conviction when he longs to order his cause before God, and the gospel answers it: the believer's plea is not his own case at all but an Advocate with the Father.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plea as that which is alleged in support or defense; in law, the answer of the defendant to the plaintiff's declaration.
webster_full: PLEA, n. In law, that which is alleged by a party in support of his demand; the answer of the defendant to the plaintiff's declaration.
PLEA, n. A cause in court; a lawsuit, or a criminal process.
PLEA, n. That which is alleged in defense or justification; an excuse; an apology.
PLEAD, v.i. To argue in support of a claim, or in defense against the claim of another.
ADVOCATE, n. One who pleads the cause of another in a court of law; an intercessor.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 17:8

If there arise a matter too hard for thee in judgment, between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke, being matters of controversy within thy gates: then shalt thou arise, and get thee up into the place which the LORD thy God shall choose;
Deuteronomy 17:9
And thou shalt come unto the priests the Levites, and unto the judge that shall be in those days, and enquire; and they shall shew thee the sentence of judgment:
Job 23:4
I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments.
1 John 2:1
My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous:
corruption_summary: Justice is increasingly measured by the identity of the parties rather than the merits of the cause, where the law of Deuteronomy 17 sends every hard plea to one court under one standard, judged without respect of persons.
corruption_paragraphs: The oldest corruption of a plea is deciding it by who is pleading. Scripture forbids it in both directions with unusual care: a judge shall not respect the person of the mighty, and he shall not countenance a poor man in his cause either. Deuteronomy 17 builds the whole appellate structure on the assumption that a plea has merits which can be found out, that some matters are simply too hard for a local court, and that the remedy is more competent judgment under God rather than a verdict distributed according to the standing of the parties. Where that assumption dies, courts stop weighing pleas and start counting them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the believer's own plea before God. Job wanted to order his cause and fill his mouth with arguments, and every honest man discovers that his best plea is not strong enough. The gospel does not improve the plea; it changes the pleader. If any man sin, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous — and the plea entered on our behalf is his blood and righteousness, which no court in heaven or earth can overrule.
roots_summary: Hebrew din (H1779), a cause or judgment; riyb (H7379), a controversy or suit; mishpat (H4941), judgment; Greek parakletos (G3875), an advocate.
roots_lines: Hebrew din (H1779) — a cause, a plea, a judgment; the plea and plea of Deuteronomy 17:8.
Hebrew riyb (H7379) — a strife, a controversy at law; matters of controversy within thy gates.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, the sentence of a court, and the justice it should embody.
Hebrew nega (H5061) — a stroke, a plague; the third class of hard cases in the same verse.
Greek parakletos (G3875) — one called alongside, an advocate; the believer's plea in 1 John 2:1.
usage: “Between blood and blood, between plea and plea” — three classes of hard cases.
“A matter too hard for thee in judgment” — the reason for a higher court.
“We have an Advocate with the Father” — the plea that cannot fail.

pos: v.t. (to name; to call by a particular appellation)
etymology: Latin terminus, a boundary or limit; hence a word that marks the bounds of a thing, and so a name. The Authorized Version uses the verb once, in one of the great renaming promises of Isaiah.
biblical_def: The single use is a promise that a people's name will be taken from them and replaced: “Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate: but thou shalt be called Hephzibah, and thy land Beulah: for the LORD delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married” (Isaiah 62:4). Two names of shame are cancelled and two names of favour given, and the ground of the change is stated in the middle of the verse: for the LORD delighteth in thee. The new name is not a description Zion earned but a declaration God made. Scripture is full of this — Abram to Abraham, Jacob to Israel, Simon to Peter, and the promise of a white stone with a new name written which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it. To be termed is to be placed within a boundary by the one with the authority to draw it, which is why the naming of things is never a neutral act.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines term as a limit or boundary; a word by which a thing is expressed; and as a verb, to name, to call, to denominate.
webster_full: TERM, n. A limit; a bound or boundary; the extremity of any thing; that which limits its extent.
TERM, n. A word or expression; that which fixes or determines ideas; the proper word by which a thing is expressed.
TERM, v.t. To name; to call; to denominate.
DENOMINATE, v.t. To name; to give a name or epithet to; to style.
NAME, n. That by which a thing is called; the sound or combination of sounds used to express an idea or any material substance.
scriptures: Isaiah 62:4

Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate: but thou shalt be called Hephzibah, and thy land Beulah: for the LORD delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married.
Isaiah 62:2
And the Gentiles shall see thy righteousness, and all kings thy glory: and thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the LORD shall name.
Genesis 17:5
Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for a father of many nations have I made thee. Abraham: that is, Father of a great multitude
Revelation 2:17

He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.
corruption_summary: Naming is now claimed as a private right — each person the author of what he shall be termed — where Scripture makes naming an act of authority, and the only name that finally holds is the one God gives.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning conviction is that a person names himself: identity is self-declared, and to term someone otherwise is an injury. Scripture treats naming as an exercise of authority throughout, from Adam naming the beasts to God renaming Abram and Jacob. The authority is real, and so is the limit on it — no creature can term himself into a nature he does not possess. Isaiah 62 is the standing refutation of both errors, the despairing and the self-inventing: Zion could not shake off the name Forsaken by insisting on another, and God removed it by a word, because the LORD delighteth in thee was a fact before it was a title.

That is also the pastoral comfort in the verse, and it is considerable. Many believers carry names given them by circumstance, by failure, or by people who meant them harm — Forsaken and Desolate are not abstractions. The promise is not that they should term themselves something better, which they cannot make true, but that God terms them otherwise on the ground of his own delight and his own covenant. Revelation carries it to the end: a new name written in a white stone, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.
roots_summary: Hebrew amar (H559), to say or call; qara (H7121), to call by name; Hephzibah (H2657), my delight is in her; Beulah (H1166), married.
roots_lines: Hebrew amar (H559) — to say, to call; the verb the AV renders termed in Isaiah 62:4.
Hebrew qara (H7121) — to call, to name, to proclaim; thou shalt be called Hephzibah.
Hebrew Hephtsiybahh (H2657) — my delight is in her; the name that cancels Forsaken.
Hebrew Beulah (H1166) — married, owned as a wife; the name that cancels Desolate.
Hebrew azab (H5800) — to forsake, to leave; the old name God takes away.
usage: “Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken” — a name cancelled by decree.
“For the LORD delighteth in thee” — the ground of the new name.
“A new name written” — the naming that outlasts every other.

etymology: Latin notitia, knowledge, from noscere, to know. The Authorized Version uses the word twice, once of a people observing their king's conduct and once of a church given advance word about a collection.
biblical_def: After Abner's death David refused to eat till the sun went down, and the narrator records the effect: “And all the people took notice of it, and it pleased them: as whatsoever the king did pleased all the people” (2 Samuel 3:36). The nation was watching its king in a matter of grief, and his fasting settled a suspicion that could have split the kingdom. The other use is administrative and just as instructive. Paul sends brethren ahead to Corinth about the collection for the saints, “that they would go before unto you, and make up beforehand your bounty, whereof ye had notice before, that the same might be ready, as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness” (2 Corinthians 9:5). Advance notice is given precisely so that the giving will not be extracted under pressure on the day. Between the two verses lies the whole biblical attitude to being observed: leaders are watched and should expect to be, and generosity is planned rather than squeezed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines notice as observation by the eye or the mind; and also, information or intelligence communicated, especially beforehand.
webster_full: NOTICE, n. Observation by the eye or by the other senses; as, to take notice of the appearance of the sky.
NOTICE, n. Information; intelligence by whatever means communicated; knowledge given or received.
NOTICE, n. Previous intimation; warning; as, the army had notice of the enemy's designs.
OBSERVE, v.t. To see or behold with some attention; to notice; to regard attentively.
BOUNTY, n. Liberality in bestowing gifts and favors; generosity; munificence.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 3:36
And all the people took notice of it, and it pleased them: as whatsoever the king did pleased all the people. pleased
2 Corinthians 9:5

Therefore I thought it necessary to exhort the brethren, that they would go before unto you, and make up beforehand your bounty, whereof ye had notice before, that the same might be ready, as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness.
2 Corinthians 9:7
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
1 Timothy 5:25
Likewise also the good works of some are manifest beforehand; and they that are otherwise cannot be hid.
corruption_summary: Giving is now commonly raised by emotional pressure applied in the moment, against an apostle who sent notice ahead precisely so that the gift would be bounty and not covetousness.
corruption_paragraphs: Fund-raising technique has largely settled on the opposite of 2 Corinthians 9:5. The appeal is made when feeling is highest, the decision is asked for on the spot, and the pressure of the room does work that conviction should have done. Paul sends men ahead with notice so that the Corinthians can make their bounty up beforehand — deliberately, at leisure, out of a settled purpose — and he names the alternative bluntly: a gift gathered any other way is as of covetousness, grasping dressed as generosity. Two verses later he states the rule that every appeal should be built on: every man according as he purposeth in his heart, not grudgingly, or of necessity, for God loveth a cheerful giver.

The other side of the word is the fact of being observed. All the people took notice of what David did with his dinner, and a kingdom's confidence turned on it. Leaders in the church are told plainly that good works are manifest beforehand and those that are otherwise cannot be hid. That is not a call to perform for the watching, which Christ condemns, but a sober recognition that a public man's private habits are rarely private for long, and that people rightly read a leader's integrity from the small things he does when he thinks the matter minor.
roots_summary: Hebrew nakar (H5234), to recognize or regard; Greek prokataggello and proepaggello (G4279), to announce beforehand; eulogia (G2129), a bounty or blessing.
roots_lines: Hebrew nakar (H5234) — to regard, discern, recognize; the people took notice of David's fast.
Hebrew yatab (H3190) — to be good, to please; it pleased them, as whatsoever the king did.
Greek proepaggello (G4279) — to promise or announce beforehand; the notice sent to Corinth.
Greek eulogia (G2129) — a blessing, hence a bounty; the planned gift as against covetousness.
Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, greediness; what a squeezed gift amounts to.
usage: “All the people took notice of it” — a kingdom reading its king.
“Whereof ye had notice before” — giving planned, not extracted.
“As a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness” — the reason for the notice.

pos: n. (position; the place where a thing is set)
etymology: Latin situs, a site or position. In the Authorized Version the word is never about circumstances in the modern sense; it means literal position on the ground — where a city sits, and how it sits.
biblical_def: The men of Jericho bring Elisha a problem that is exactly a matter of position: “Behold, I pray thee, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord seeth: but the water is naught, and the ground barren” (2 Kings 2:19). Everything about the site was right except the one thing that makes a site habitable, and the prophet healed the spring with salt in a new cruse, saying the LORD had healed these waters. The other use is the loftiest description of Jerusalem in the Psalms: “Beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth, is mount Zion, on the sides of the north, the city of the great King” (Psalm 48:2). The beauty named there is not architecture but placement — where God set the city. Scripture thus uses the word for something a city cannot choose about itself and cannot change: the position given it. Zion's glory is that the great King chose to set his house there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines situation as position; seat; location; and the place where a thing is set with respect to surrounding objects.
webster_full: SITUATION, n. Position; seat; location in respect to something else; as, the situation of a city on a river.
SITUATION, n. State; condition; as, a man in easy or embarrassed situation.
SITUATION, n. Place; office; as, a situation under the government.
SITE, n. Situation; local position; as the site of a city or of a house.
PLEASANT, a. Pleasing; agreeable; grateful to the mind or to the senses.
scriptures: 2 Kings 2:19
And the men of the city said unto Elisha, Behold, I pray thee, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord seeth: but the water is naught, and the ground barren.
2 Kings 2:21
And he went forth unto the spring of the waters, and cast the salt in there, and said, Thus saith the LORD, I have healed these waters; there shall not be from thence any more death or barren land.
Psalm 48:2
Beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth, is mount Zion, on the sides of the north, the city of the great King.
Psalm 48:1
A Song and Psalm for the sons of Korah. Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, in the mountain of his holiness.
corruption_summary: The word has shifted from position given to circumstances suffered, and with it the modern habit of explaining a man wholly by his situation; Scripture uses it of a place God appointed, and of a bad spring God healed.
corruption_paragraphs: In current speech a person's situation explains him: he is a product of where he finds himself, and both his conduct and his prospects are read off his circumstances. The KJV never uses the word that way. A situation is a position, and in both occurrences it is a position assigned rather than achieved. Zion is beautiful for situation because God set his city there; Jericho's situation was pleasant because the site was good. What is wrong at Jericho is not the situation but the water, and the remedy is not relocation but healing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is providential placement. The Athenians were told that God determined the times before appointed and the bounds of men's habitation, and Paul told the Corinthians that as God hath distributed to every man, so let him walk. A believer's situation — his country, his family, his century, his employment — is a station given him to be faithful in, not an accident to be escaped before obedience can begin. And where the ground is barren and the water naught, the God of 2 Kings 2 still heals springs.
roots_summary: Hebrew mowshab (H4186), a seat or dwelling-place; nowph (H5131), elevation, beautiful for situation; qiryah (H7151), a city; ra (H7451), bad or naught.
roots_lines: Hebrew mowshab (H4186) — a seat, a site, a dwelling; the situation of the city in 2 Kings 2:19.
Hebrew nowph (H5131) — elevation, height; beautiful for situation in Psalm 48:2.
Hebrew ra (H7451) — bad, evil, naught; the water that spoiled a pleasant site.
Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal, to mend; what the LORD did to the waters of Jericho.
Hebrew Tsiyown (H6726) — Zion; the city of the great King, glorious in its placement.
usage: “The situation of this city is pleasant... but the water is naught” — the one flaw.
“Beautiful for situation... is mount Zion” — glory in where God set it.
“The city of the great King” — what makes a situation glorious.
